issues.legal_issue: A statutory corporation's land allotment does not create an enforceable lease where a formal lease deed is required and the proposed lessee fails to execute it.
material_facts: The allotment was expressly subject to execution of a formal lease deed, and the corporation sent a draft deed for execution.
The recipient took advance possession but did not execute the deed despite repeated requests.
The recipient also failed to pay the required instalments, and the corporation later resumed the land.
The case reached the Supreme Court in appeals challenging a High Court direction to grant a lease.
issues.conclusion: No concluded or enforceable lease arose, and the recipient acquired no right to compel execution of the lease deed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 33 of the Orissa Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation Act, 1980 permitted disposal of land subject to the State Government's directions and the applicable terms. Where a statutory body must act through a prescribed formal instrument, failure to execute that instrument prevents a binding contract from arising. The Court relied on Bhikraj Jaipuria v. Union of India, AIR 1962 SC 113, and also referred to Laliteshwar Prasad Sahi v. Bateshwar Prasad, AIR 1968 SC 580, Karamshi Jethabhai Somayya v. State of Bombay, AIR 1964 SC 1714, and Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1968 SC 1218, concerning formalities for government contracts and the absence of estoppel or ratification where mandatory formalities are unmet.

predicates.statutory_body_disposed_of_land_subject_: A statutory body offered land on terms requiring a formal instrument before the disposition could be completed.
predicates.recipient_failed_to_execute_required_ins: The recipient did not execute the formal instrument despite being asked to do so.
predicates.recipient_failed_to_perform_allocation_o: The recipient did not carry out required obligations associated with the land allocation, including payment obligations.

issues.definition: When a statutory body makes a land disposition subject to a required formal instrument and the recipient fails to execute it and perform the allocation obligations, an appeal from a writ direction does not result in an enforceable lease.

issues.legal_issue: A cure period in proposed lease terms does not prevent resumption where the lease was never executed, and in any event the breach remained uncured long after notice.
material_facts: The proposed lease terms allowed a lessee time after written notice to remedy a breach.
No lease deed was executed, so the lessor-lessee relationship never came into existence.
The recipient was asked to execute the deed and remedy its defaults, but did not do so for several years before resumption.
The case reached the Supreme Court in appeals challenging a High Court direction to grant a lease.
issues.conclusion: The proposed lease's cure-period provision did not bar resumption of the land.
issues.legal_principle: The cure provision was part of the terms to be inserted in a lease deed that was never executed, and therefore it did not become operative. The Court also concluded that, even if the provision applied, the recipient had been given more than the specified cure period and had not remedied the breach.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a writ court's direction to grant a land lease.
predicates.lease_deed_never_executed: The parties did not execute the formal lease deed that was to contain the proposed cure-period term.
predicates.breach_remained_uncured_long_after_writt: The recipient did not remedy the identified defaults for a substantial time after receiving written notice.

issues.definition: When the lease deed containing the proposed cure term was never executed and the recipient left the breach uncured long after written notice, the cure period did not prevent resumption.

issues.legal_issue: A payment made under an unenforceable land arrangement may be retained or applied as compensation for use and occupation where the recipient possessed the land and failed to fulfil its obligations.
material_facts: The recipient paid an initial amount and took possession of the land.
It did not execute the lease deed or pay the remaining instalments, and continued to retain possession until the land was resumed.
The corporation forfeited the initial payment and applied it toward compensation for use and occupation and damages.
The case reached the Supreme Court in appeals challenging a High Court direction to grant a lease.
issues.conclusion: The forfeiture and adjustment of the initial payment toward compensation for use and occupation and damages was justified; the recipient was also liable for compensation for retaining possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides for compensation where a person lawfully does something for another without intending to act gratuitously and the other enjoys the benefit. It can apply despite the absence of an enforceable contract, but does not permit specific performance of the void contract. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal and Sons, AIR 1962 SC 779, New Marine Coal Co. (Bengal) Private Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1964 SC 152, and Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1968 SC 1218.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot compel a statutory body to grant a land disposition that was subject to a required formal instrument when no relied-upon assurance was given.
material_facts: The proposed land allocation was expressly subject to execution of a formal lease deed.
The State withdrew an earlier offer of equity participation before the direction to allot land was issued.
The recipient did not establish that an assurance had been given on which it acted.
The case reached the Supreme Court in appeals challenging a High Court direction to grant a lease.
issues.conclusion: Promissory estoppel did not apply and could not require the corporation to execute the lease.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory body can act only in the prescribed manner, and an assurance inconsistent with required formalities cannot bind it. The Court relied on Mumbai International Airport Private Ltd. v. Golden Chariot Airport, (2010) 10 SCC 422, and on the principle stated in Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1968 SC 1218, that estoppel or ratification cannot cure non-compliance with mandatory formalities protecting the public.

issues.definition: When a statutory body must use a formal instrument and the recipient did not rely on an assurance, promissory estoppel cannot compel the disposition.

issues.legal_issue: Equitable or writ relief cannot require a statutory body to grant land to an applicant that left its obligations unperformed through prolonged neglect, particularly after third-party rights intervened.
material_facts: The recipient failed for years to execute the lease deed, pay the required instalments, or remedy its defaults, and gave no adequate explanation for its inaction.
It made no substantial development on the land and did not establish its asserted expenditure.
After resumption, portions of the land were allotted to other industries and possession and lease arrangements were completed.
The High Court directed the corporation to lease the remaining land to the recipient, and the corporation appealed.
issues.conclusion: The recipient had no legal or equitable right to the directed lease, the High Court's direction was impermissible, and the writ petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Where a beneficial right depends on acts being performed in a stated manner or time, those conditions must generally be strictly observed, and equity will not relieve against breach absent circumstances such as fraud, accident, or surprise. The Court relied on Khela Banerjee v. City Montessori School, (2012) 7 SCC 261, and Raj Kishore v. Prem Singh, (2011) 1 SCC 657, including the passage from Halsbury's Laws of England on strict observance of conditions. It also held that a writ cannot be used to perpetuate an illegality or override intervening third-party rights.

issues.definition: When a recipient in an appeal from a writ direction leaves required obligations unperformed through unexplained prolonged neglect, and makes no substantial development or third-party rights have intervened, equitable writ relief directing a grant of the land is unavailable.
